## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Deep Learning in Practice / Advanced Deep Learning
  Official title       Deep Learning in Practice / Advanced Deep Learning
  Instructors          G. CHARPIAT (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 12 h, tutorials 12 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Deep Learning
  Language             Not displayed; the course description on master-mva.com is written in English
  Assessment           “The evaluation of the course is based on 6 exercises” (master-mva.com, *Mode de validation*); the practical and theoretical exercises in PyTorch that accompany the lectures are evaluated (*Organisation des séances*); no weights displayed · Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment)
  Prerequisites        The “Introduction to Deep Learning” course by Vincent Lepetit (semester 1); notions in machine learning, Bayesian statistics, analysis and differential calculus; basic knowledge of Python and PyTorch (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student who has taken a first deep-learning course, can train a network in PyTorch, and now wants to know why training works, when it fails, and how to make it work on data that is small, noisy, biased or governed by physics.

**Empirical first**: a network with 38 410 parameters reaches 97 % test accuracy on 1 257 handwritten digits, yet it fits the same digits with randomly shuffled labels just as perfectly, at 9 % test accuracy (ch. 1). A classical capacity bound cannot tell the two runs apart; this course explains what can, and what to do in practice.

Deep learning works far better than its classical theory predicts, yet networks are hard to train, hard to explain and easily biased. Real problems rarely fit the textbook setting either: data are scarce or noisy, and physical laws are known. This course gives mathematical tools for these practical aspects. It continues the semester-1 [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) course and shares tools with [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html), [Multimodal Explainable AI](../s2-multimodal-xai/index.html), [Responsible Machine Learning](../s2-responsible-ml/index.html) and [Learning Physical Phenomena](../s2-physics-learning-uq/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Explain why parameter counts and uniform capacity bounds fail to predict the test error of deep networks, and reproduce the random-label experiment.
-   Prove that over-parameterised least squares trained by gradient descent converges to the minimum-norm interpolator, and reproduce double descent.
-   Choose an architecture from the symmetries of the data: residual blocks, attention, Deep Sets for sets and graph attention for graphs.
-   Compute and criticise attribution maps: gradients, integrated gradients, Grad-CAM, occlusion, with sanity checks.
-   Audit a model for an undesired dependence on a sensitive attribute, with fairness criteria and counterfactual tests, and reduce it.
-   Train with few labels, coarse labels or noisy labels, using semi-supervised losses, loss correction, robust losses and multiple-instance pooling.
-   Build invariances and physical laws into a model: group convolutions, physics-informed losses for PDEs, Hamiltonian networks.
-   Derive and implement the three classical deep generative models: variational auto-encoders, GANs and normalizing flows.
-   Tune hyper-parameters automatically with random search, Bayesian optimisation and successive halving.
-   State a generalisation bound for networks, and certify a prediction formally with Lipschitz bounds, interval propagation or a mixed-integer program.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com starts from a diagnosis. Despite impressive results, deep learning methods are still poorly understood, networks are often difficult to train, and their results are black boxes. This is a problem given the societal impact of machine learning: it assists decisions in medicine, hiring and bank loans. Real problems also rarely fit the assumptions of the best-known academic work, for instance in data quantity and quality.

The course aims at insights and tools for these practical aspects, based on mathematical concepts. It first emphasises the gap between practice and classical theory, for instance in the number of parameters, and reconciles them with recent theoretical advances.

After a review of recent architectures, it studies visualisation techniques and checks that undesired biases of the data set are not reproduced, for instance a sensitivity to gender when matching CVs to job offers. It then turns to practical issues of training: data quantity, small or big; applications to reinforcement learning and to physical problems; and automatic hyper-parameter tuning.

### Course outline

-   **Review: risk, gradients and the training loop** — empirical risk, bias and variance, backpropagation, the descent lemma and a PyTorch training loop.
-   **Deep learning versus classical machine learning and optimisation** — why parameter counts mislead, over-parameterised optimisation, implicit bias, double descent, mimic learning.
-   **Architectures** — residual blocks and normalisation, attention, networks on sets (Deep Sets) and on graphs (graph attention).
-   **Interpretability, visualisation and biases** — attribution maps and their axioms, sanity checks, fairness criteria, counterfactual audits and debiasing.
-   **Small or noisy data** — the forms of weak supervision, semi-supervised learning, label noise, multiple-instance learning and the big-data regime.
-   **Modelling: deep learning, physics and control** — invariances, physics-informed losses for PDEs, Hamiltonian structure, deep reinforcement learning.
-   **Generative models** — variational auto-encoders, generative adversarial networks and normalizing flows.
-   **Auto-ML** — random search, Bayesian optimisation, successive halving, architecture search.
-   **Guarantees?** — generalisation bounds for networks and formal verification of their predictions.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — feature learning, mechanistic interpretability, fairness, neural operators and scalable verification (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read the chapters in order: each one uses only the previous ones. Chapter 0 can be skimmed by a reader fluent in backpropagation and maximum likelihood.
-   After each session, do the exercises of its row in the plan, then run the Python block of the chapter and change one setting: a width, a noise rate, a step size.
-   The Python environment is the one of the [scientific Python refresher](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html): NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch on CPU. Every block uses synthetic data or the digits data set bundled with scikit-learn.
-   Keep a page of formulas: the minimum-norm interpolator, the Deep Sets form, integrated gradients, the forward loss correction, the ELBO, the change of variables, expected improvement, and the PAC-Bayes bound.
-   For the evaluated exercises of the official assessment, the [practical sheets](#projects) of the *Projects and assessment* section are a good rehearsal.

## 0. Review: risk, gradients and the training loop {#ch0}

Training a network means minimising an empirical risk with stochastic gradients computed by backpropagation. This chapter recalls the four M1 facts behind that sentence; every later chapter uses them.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Risk, empirical risk, generalisation gap]{.tag}
Data $(x, y)$ follow an unknown distribution $P$, a predictor $f$ maps inputs to outputs, and a loss $\ell$ compares the prediction with the label. The **risk** and, for a sample $S$ of $n$ independent pairs, the **empirical risk** are
$$
R(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim P}\, \ell(f(x), y), \qquad \widehat R_S(f) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f(x_i), y_i).
$$
Training minimises $\widehat R_S$ over a class $\{f_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}^p\}$. For the trained predictor $f_S$, the **generalisation gap** is $R(f_S) - \widehat R_S(f_S)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Bias–variance decomposition]{.tag}
Let $y = f^\star(x) + \varepsilon$ with $\mathbb{E}\varepsilon = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var}\varepsilon = \sigma^2$, the noise independent of the sample. Write $\bar f(x) = \mathbb{E}_S f_S(x)$. At a fixed input $x$, with the squared loss,
$$
\mathbb{E}_{S,\varepsilon}\big(y - f_S(x)\big)^2 = \sigma^2 + \big(f^\star(x) - \bar f(x)\big)^2 + \operatorname{Var}_S f_S(x).
$$

::: proof
Write $y - f_S = \varepsilon + (f^\star - \bar f) + (\bar f - f_S)$ and expand the square.

-   The cross terms with $\varepsilon$ vanish: $\varepsilon$ is centred and independent of $S$.
-   The cross term $2(f^\star - \bar f)\,\mathbb{E}_S(\bar f - f_S)$ vanishes by definition of $\bar f$.

The three squares that remain are the noise, the squared bias and the variance. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The classical reading: a richer model lowers the bias and raises the variance, so the test error is U-shaped in the number of parameters. Chapter 1 shows where this picture breaks.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Softmax cross-entropy and backpropagation]{.tag}
For logits $z \in \mathbb{R}^K$, probabilities $p = \operatorname{softmax}(z)$ and label $y$, the loss $\mathcal{L} = -\log p_y$ has gradient
$$
\nabla_z \mathcal{L} = p - e_y .
$$
For an affine layer $z = W a + b$ with $\delta = \nabla_z \mathcal{L}$, the gradients are $\nabla_W \mathcal{L} = \delta\, a^\top$, $\nabla_b \mathcal{L} = \delta$ and $\nabla_a \mathcal{L} = W^\top \delta$.

::: proof
Since $-\log p_y = -z_y + \log \sum_k e^{z_k}$, the derivative in $z_k$ is $-\mathbb{1}[k = y] + p_k$. The affine formulas are the chain rule applied to $z_j = \sum_k W_{jk} a_k + b_j$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Backpropagation applies these rules from the loss back to the input, layer by layer. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation does it for any computational graph, at the cost of a few forward passes.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Descent lemma]{.tag}
If $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, a gradient step of size $\eta$ satisfies
$$
f\big(\theta - \eta \nabla f(\theta)\big) \le f(\theta) - \eta \Big(1 - \frac{L \eta}{2}\Big) \|\nabla f(\theta)\|^2 .
$$
With $\eta = 1/L$ the decrease is at least $\|\nabla f(\theta)\|^2 / (2L)$.

::: proof
By Taylor's formula with integral remainder and the Lipschitz gradient,
$$
f(\theta + d) \le f(\theta) + \nabla f(\theta)^\top d + \frac{L}{2}\|d\|^2 .
$$
Take $d = -\eta \nabla f(\theta)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Stochastic gradient descent replaces the full gradient by the average over a random mini-batch of size $B$. This estimate is unbiased, and its variance decreases like $1/B$.

Code 0.1 trains a one-hidden-layer network on the digits data set of scikit-learn (1 797 images of $8 \times 8$ pixels) with mini-batch SGD and momentum.

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(0)

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)                     # 1797 images 8x8, 10 classes
X = torch.tensor(X / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)
y = torch.tensor(y)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(64, 256), torch.nn.ReLU(),
                            torch.nn.Linear(256, 10))
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1, momentum=0.9)
loss_fn = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()                    # softmax + negative log-likelihood

def accuracy(Xs, ys):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (model(Xs).argmax(1) == ys).float().mean().item()

for epoch in range(30):
    perm = torch.randperm(len(Xtr))
    for i in range(0, len(Xtr), 64):                     # mini-batches of 64
        idx = perm[i:i + 64]
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(model(Xtr[idx]), ytr[idx])
        loss.backward()                                  # reverse-mode autodiff
        opt.step()
    if epoch % 10 == 9:
        print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:2d}  train loss {loss_fn(model(Xtr), ytr).item():.4f}"
              f"  train acc {accuracy(Xtr, ytr):.3f}  test acc {accuracy(Xte, yte):.3f}")
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()), " training points:", len(Xtr))
```

The network has 19 210 parameters for 1 257 training points. After 30 epochs it fits the training set exactly, and its test accuracy is
$$
\text{train accuracy} = 1.000, \qquad \text{test accuracy} = 0.974 .
$$
More parameters than data, zero training error, and yet good generalisation: this is the puzzle of ch. 1.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 0
:::

-   Training minimises the empirical risk; what matters is the risk, and their difference is the generalisation gap.
-   The squared error splits into noise, squared bias and variance (Proposition 0.2).
-   The softmax cross-entropy has gradient $p - e_y$ in the logits; backpropagation chains such local rules.
-   A step $1/L$ on an $L$-smooth function decreases it by at least $\|\nabla f\|^2/(2L)$.
::::

## 1. Deep learning versus classical machine learning and optimisation {#ch1}

Classical learning theory controls the test error by the size of the model class, and classical optimisation fears non-convex losses. Deep networks defy both: they have more parameters than data and non-convex losses, yet they train easily and generalise. This chapter makes the gap precise, then presents the results that reduce it.

### 1.1 Parameter counts and capacity

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.1 — Occam bound for a finite class]{.tag}
Let the loss take values in $[0, 1]$ and let $\mathcal{F}$ be finite. With probability at least $1 - \delta$ over the sample, every $f \in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies
$$
R(f) \le \widehat R_S(f) + \sqrt{\frac{\ln |\mathcal{F}| + \ln(1/\delta)}{2n}} .
$$

::: proof
For a fixed $f$, the losses $\ell(f(x_i), y_i)$ are independent and bounded, so Hoeffding's inequality gives
$$
\mathbb{P}\big(R(f) - \widehat R_S(f) > t\big) \le e^{-2 n t^2}.
$$
A union bound over the $|\mathcal{F}|$ functions gives the failure probability $|\mathcal{F}|\, e^{-2nt^2}$. Setting it to $\delta$ and solving for $t$ gives the bound. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A network with $p$ parameters stored in 32-bit floats belongs to a class of at most $2^{32p}$ functions, so $\ln|\mathcal{F}| \approx 22.2\, p$. The bound says nothing unless $n$ is much larger than $22\, p$. VC-dimension bounds behave the same way: for ReLU networks the VC dimension grows like the number of parameters times the depth, up to a logarithm (Bartlett and coauthors, 2019).

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — Fitting random labels]{.tag}
Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht and Vinyals (2017) trained standard image classifiers on CIFAR-10 with labels replaced by random ones. The networks reached zero training error, with test error at chance. Code 1.1 repeats the experiment on the digits.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
torch.set_num_threads(1)

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X = torch.tensor(X / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, torch.tensor(y), test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
y_rand = ytr[torch.randperm(len(ytr), generator=g)]      # labels shuffled: no signal left

for name, labels in [("true labels", ytr), ("random labels", y_rand)]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(64, 512), torch.nn.ReLU(),
                              torch.nn.Linear(512, 10))  # 38 410 parameters for 1257 points
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    for step in range(500):                              # full-batch training
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(Xtr), labels)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        tr = (net(Xtr).argmax(1) == labels).float().mean().item()
        te = (net(Xte).argmax(1) == yte).float().mean().item()
    print(f"{name:13s}  train acc {tr:.3f}  test acc {te:.3f}  final loss {loss.item():.4f}")
```

The same network, optimiser and number of steps give
$$
\text{true labels: train } 1.000,\ \text{test } 0.972; \qquad \text{random labels: train } 1.000,\ \text{test } 0.089 .
$$

The class of functions can fit anything, so a bound that depends only on the class must be vacuous for the true labels as well. What differs between the two runs is the data and the solution found. Useful explanations therefore depend on the algorithm and on the solution, through norms, margins or flatness (ch. 8).

### 1.2 Over-parameterised optimisation

The training loss of a network is not convex, yet gradient descent drives it to zero in the over-parameterised regime. A convenient sufficient condition replaces convexity.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition and linear convergence]{.tag}
Let $f \ge 0$ be $L$-smooth with $\min f = 0$, and assume the PL inequality: for all $\theta$, $\frac12 \|\nabla f(\theta)\|^2 \ge \mu f(\theta)$. Gradient descent with step $1/L$ satisfies
$$
f(\theta_t) \le \Big(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\Big)^t f(\theta_0).
$$

::: proof
The descent lemma (Proposition 0.4) and the PL inequality give
$$
f(\theta_{t+1}) \le f(\theta_t) - \frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla f(\theta_t)\|^2 \le \Big(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\Big) f(\theta_t).
$$
Iterate $t$ times. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Under PL, every stationary point is a global minimum, without convexity. For the squared loss of a model $F : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^n$ on the training set, with residual $r = F(\theta) - y$ and Jacobian $J$, the gradient is $J^\top r$.

Hence the PL constant is the smallest eigenvalue of the $n \times n$ matrix $J J^\top$:
$$
\|\nabla f\|^2 = \|J^\top r\|^2 \ge \lambda_{\min}(J J^\top)\, \|r\|^2 = 2\, \lambda_{\min}(J J^\top)\, f .
$$
This matrix can be non-singular only if $p \ge n$. Liu, Zhu and Belkin (2022) show that, for wide enough networks, it stays well conditioned in a ball around the initialisation that contains the whole trajectory.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — Linearised dynamics and the neural tangent kernel]{.tag}
Replace the model by its linearisation $F(\theta_0) + J_0 (\theta - \theta_0)$ at initialisation, and run gradient flow on the squared loss. The training residual then evolves as
$$
r(t) = e^{-K t}\, r(0), \qquad K = J_0 J_0^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}.
$$

::: proof
The flow is $\dot\theta = -J_0^\top r$, and the linearised residual changes as $\dot r = J_0 \dot\theta = -K r$, a linear differential equation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

$K$ is the Gram matrix, on the training set, of the **neural tangent kernel**
$$
k(x, x') = \nabla_\theta f_{\theta_0}(x)^\top \nabla_\theta f_{\theta_0}(x').
$$
Jacot, Gabriel and Hongler (2018) proved that, as the width tends to infinity under a suitable scaling, this kernel is deterministic and stays constant during training. The network then trains like kernel regression: the *lazy* regime.

Each eigendirection of $K$ decays at the rate of its eigenvalue, so the smooth components of the target, with large eigenvalues, are fitted first. Finite networks leave the lazy regime and learn features; ch. 9 returns to this.

### 1.3 Implicit bias: which interpolator?

With more parameters than data, infinitely many parameter vectors fit the data exactly. The training algorithm, not the loss, selects one of them.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — Gradient descent finds the minimum-norm interpolator]{.tag}
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ have rank $n < p$, and run gradient descent on $f(\theta) = \frac12\|A\theta - b\|^2$ from $\theta_0$, with a step $0 < \eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}(A^\top A)$. Then
$$
\theta_t \longrightarrow \theta_0 + A^+ (b - A\theta_0), \qquad A^+ = A^\top (A A^\top)^{-1}.
$$
From $\theta_0 = 0$, the limit $A^+ b$ is the interpolator of smallest Euclidean norm.

::: proof
1.  Each step adds $-\eta A^\top (A\theta_t - b)$, a vector of the row space of $A$. Hence $\theta_t - \theta_0$ stays in $\operatorname{range}(A^\top)$.
2.  The residual $r_t = A\theta_t - b$ satisfies $r_{t+1} = (I - \eta A A^\top) r_t$. The eigenvalues of $A A^\top$ lie in $(0, \lambda_{\max}]$, so every factor $|1 - \eta\lambda|$ is below 1 and $r_t \to 0$.
3.  The limit interpolates and differs from $\theta_0$ by a vector of $\operatorname{range}(A^\top)$. Since that space meets $\ker A$ only at 0, the limit is unique and equals the stated point.
4.  Any interpolator is $A^+ b + v$ with $v \in \ker A$. As $A^+ b \in \operatorname{range}(A^\top) \perp \ker A$, its squared norm is $\|A^+ b\|^2 + \|v\|^2$, minimal at $v = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The algorithm thus regularises implicitly. For linear classifiers on separable data, gradient descent on the logistic loss converges in direction to the maximum-margin separator (Soudry and coauthors, 2018): again a norm is minimised without being written in the loss.

### 1.4 Double descent and the jamming transition

::: ex
[Example 1.6 — Double descent with random features]{.tag}
Take $n = 100$ training points in dimension 20, a target $\tanh(\beta^\top x)$ plus noise, and $p$ random ReLU features with a frozen first layer. The second layer is the minimum-norm least-squares fit of Theorem 1.5. Code 1.2 reports the median test error over 20 draws.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, n, n_test = 20, 100, 2000
beta = rng.normal(size=d) / np.sqrt(d)

def data(m):
    X = rng.normal(size=(m, d))
    return X, np.tanh(X @ beta) + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=m)

def test_error(p, seeds=20):
    errs = []
    for _ in range(seeds):
        X, y = data(n)
        Xt, yt = data(n_test)
        W = rng.normal(size=(d, p)) / np.sqrt(d)          # random first layer, frozen
        F, Ft = np.maximum(X @ W, 0), np.maximum(Xt @ W, 0)
        a = np.linalg.pinv(F) @ y                         # least squares, minimum norm if p > n
        errs.append(np.mean((Ft @ a - yt) ** 2))
    return np.median(errs)

for p in [10, 50, 80, 95, 100, 105, 120, 200, 500, 2000]:
    print(f"p = {p:5d}   p/n = {p / n:5.2f}   test MSE = {test_error(p):8.3f}")
```

The test error first follows the classical U, then explodes at the interpolation threshold, then descends again:
$$
p = 50:\ 0.163, \qquad p = n = 100:\ 7.453, \qquad p = 200:\ 0.100, \qquad p = 2000:\ 0.055 .
$$

At $p = n$ the feature matrix is square and badly conditioned, so the interpolator has a huge norm and amplifies the noise. Beyond the threshold, the minimum-norm choice among many interpolators shrinks the norm, and the variance falls. Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal (2019) named this curve *double descent*; Nakkiran and coauthors (2020) observed it in deep networks, as a function of width and of training time.

For deep networks, Geiger and coauthors (2019) call the threshold $N^\star$ at which the training set can be fitted a **jamming transition**. Beyond it, the trained output fluctuates with the random initialisation, with a size that decreases like $N^{-1/4}$ in the number of parameters $N$. The test error then decays to a plateau like $N^{-1/2}$.

At $N^\star$ itself the norm of the output function diverges, which explains the cusp of the test error. Their practical advice: at a fixed computational budget, average the outputs of several networks of intermediate size just beyond $N^\star$, which removes the fluctuations.

### 1.5 Do deep nets need to be deep? Mimic learning and distillation

Ba and Caruana (2014) trained shallow networks on TIMIT and CIFAR-10. Trained on the labels, they lose clearly to deep networks. Trained to regress the logits of a deep teacher with a squared loss, shallow networks with as many parameters come close to the teacher.

Part of the advantage of depth is therefore in learning, not only in what the network can represent. Distillation (Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, 2015) generalises mimic learning with a temperature $T$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Distillation at high temperature matches logits]{.tag}
Let $z$ and $v$ be the logits of student and teacher over $K$ classes, and $T > 0$ a temperature. Define
$$
q = \operatorname{softmax}(z/T), \qquad p = \operatorname{softmax}(v/T), \qquad C = -\sum_k p_k \log q_k .
$$
Then $\partial C / \partial z_k = (q_k - p_k)/T$. If both logit vectors have mean zero and $T$ is large compared with them,
$$
\frac{\partial C}{\partial z_k} \approx \frac{z_k - v_k}{K\, T^2},
$$
the gradient of a squared logit-matching loss.

::: proof
The first identity is Proposition 0.3 applied to the logits $z/T$, with the target distribution $p$ instead of a one-hot label.

For large $T$, $e^{z_k/T} \approx 1 + z_k/T$, so with mean-zero logits $q_k \approx (1 + z_k/T)/K$, and likewise $p_k \approx (1 + v_k/T)/K$. Subtract and divide by $T$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The logit regression of Ba and Caruana is thus the high-temperature limit of distillation (Exercise 12).

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::

-   Bounds that depend only on the size of the class are vacuous for networks: the same network fits random labels (Example 1.2).
-   Over-parameterisation makes optimisation easy: the PL inequality gives linear convergence (Theorem 1.3), and wide networks behave like their linearisation (Proposition 1.4).
-   Gradient descent picks the minimum-norm interpolator (Theorem 1.5): the algorithm regularises.
-   The test error peaks at the interpolation threshold and descends beyond it; ensembles of networks just beyond the threshold remove the fluctuations.
-   Mimic learning and distillation transfer what a deep network learnt to a smaller one.
::::

## 2. Architectures: residual networks, attention, sets and graphs {#ch2}

An architecture is a prior: it decides which functions training reaches easily, and which symmetries hold exactly. This chapter reviews the building blocks of recent architectures, then derives the structure that the symmetries of sets and graphs impose.

### 2.1 Depth that trains: residual blocks and normalisation

A residual network stacks blocks $x_{l+1} = x_l + F_l(x_l)$, where each branch $F_l$ is a small network (He, Zhang, Ren and Sun, 2016).

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.1 — Residual blocks preserve the gradient]{.tag}
Let $J_k$ be the Jacobian of the branch $F_k$ and assume $\|J_k\| \le \varepsilon < 1$ for every block. The Jacobian of $x_L$ with respect to $x_l$ is the product of the factors $I + J_k$, and all its singular values lie in
$$
\big[(1 - \varepsilon)^{L - l},\ (1 + \varepsilon)^{L - l}\big].
$$

::: proof
The chain rule gives the product. Each factor $I + J_k$ has singular values in $[1 - \varepsilon, 1 + \varepsilon]$ by Weyl's inequality. The largest singular value of a product is at most the product of the largest ones, and the smallest is at least the product of the smallest ones. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With small branches at initialisation, for instance a last layer initialised at zero in each branch, the gradient neither vanishes nor explodes through hundreds of layers.

Normalisation layers rescale pre-activations. Batch normalisation (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015) standardises each unit over the mini-batch, then applies a learnt scale and shift. Layer normalisation (Ba, Kiros and Hinton, 2016) standardises over the units of one example; transformers use it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Scale invariance under normalisation]{.tag}
Let $g(w)$ be a loss that depends on the weights $w$ of a unit only through its normalised pre-activation, so that $g(cw) = g(w)$ for every $c > 0$. Then
$$
w^\top \nabla g(w) = 0, \qquad \nabla g(cw) = \frac{1}{c}\, \nabla g(w).
$$

::: proof
Differentiate $g(cw) = g(w)$ in $c$ at $c = 1$ for the first identity, and in $w$ for the second. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Two practical consequences follow. A gradient step is orthogonal to $w$, so by Pythagoras it increases $\|w\|$. And the effective learning rate is $\eta / \|w\|^2$: weight decay, which shrinks $\|w\|$, acts on such layers as a learning-rate schedule rather than as a regulariser.

### 2.2 Attention and transformers

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Scaled dot-product attention]{.tag}
For $m$ tokens stacked in $X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}$, with queries $Q = X W_Q$, keys $K = X W_K$ of width $d_k$ and values $V = X W_V$,
$$
\operatorname{Attn}(X) = \operatorname{softmax}\Big(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big) V,
$$
the softmax acting on each row. A transformer block (Vaswani and coauthors, 2017) applies, with residual connections and layer normalisation, multi-head attention and then a two-layer network to each token.
:::

The factor $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the scores of order one: if the entries of a query and a key are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance $d_k$. Without it, the softmax saturates and its gradient vanishes.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Self-attention is permutation-equivariant]{.tag}
Without positional encodings, for every permutation matrix $P$,
$$
\operatorname{Attn}(P X) = P\, \operatorname{Attn}(X).
$$

::: proof
Permuting the tokens replaces $Q, K, V$ by $PQ, PK, PV$, so the score matrix $S$ becomes $P S P^\top$. A row-wise softmax commutes with permuting rows and columns together, and $P^\top P = I$, so the output is
$$
P \operatorname{softmax}(S) P^\top P V = P \operatorname{Attn}(X).
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Order must therefore be injected by positional encodings. A transformer is a model of sets plus positions; vision transformers apply it to the sequence of $16 \times 16$ patches of an image (Dosovitskiy and coauthors, 2021).

### 2.3 Networks on sets: Deep Sets

Point clouds, particles of a simulation or the atoms of a molecule are sets: the order in which they are listed carries no information.

::: def
[Definition 2.5 — Invariance and equivariance to permutations]{.tag}
A function $f$ of $m$ elements is **permutation-invariant** if, for every permutation $\sigma$,
$$
f(x_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(m)}) = f(x_1, \dots, x_m).
$$
A map with $m$ outputs is **permutation-equivariant** if permuting the inputs permutes the outputs in the same way.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.6 — Representation of set functions (Zaheer and coauthors, 2017)]{.tag}
Let $\mathcal{X}$ be countable. A function $f$ on the finite subsets of $\mathcal{X}$ can always be written, for some $\phi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $\rho : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, as
$$
f(S) = \rho\Big(\sum_{x \in S} \phi(x)\Big).
$$
Conversely, every function of this form is permutation-invariant.

::: proof
The converse holds because a sum does not depend on the order of its terms. For the direct part:

1.  Enumerate $\mathcal{X}$ by an injection $c : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{N}$ and set $\phi(x) = 4^{-c(x)}$.
2.  The sum over $S$ is a base-4 number whose digits are 0 or 1, the digit of position $c(x)$ being 1 exactly when $x \in S$. Distinct finite sets thus have distinct sums.
3.  Define $\rho$ on the set of sums by $\rho\big(\sum_{x \in S}\phi(x)\big) = f(S)$, which is well defined by step 2, and arbitrarily elsewhere. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For multisets with bounded multiplicities, a larger base works the same way. For continuous inputs, Wagstaff and coauthors (2019) show that continuous $\phi$ and $\rho$ need a latent dimension at least equal to the size of the set: the theorem guarantees expressivity, not economy.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Linear permutation-equivariant layers]{.tag}
A linear map $L : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is permutation-equivariant if and only if, for some scalars $a$ and $b$,
$$
L = a\, I + b\, \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top .
$$

::: proof
Equivariance means $P L = L P$ for every permutation matrix $P$, that is $L_{\sigma(i)\sigma(j)} = L_{ij}$ for all $i, j, \sigma$.

-   Permutations map any diagonal position $(i, i)$ to any other, so all diagonal entries are equal.
-   They map any off-diagonal pair $(i, j)$ to any other, so all off-diagonal entries equal one value $b$.

Hence $L = aI + b\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$, with $a + b$ on the diagonal. Conversely, $P$ commutes with $I$ and with $\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

An equivariant Deep Sets layer is thus
$$
x \mapsto \sigma\big(\lambda x + \gamma\, (\mathbf{1}^\top x)\, \mathbf{1}\big),
$$
with matrices instead of scalars when each element carries several channels. A final sum makes the network invariant. Code 2.1 learns the variance of a set of 10 numbers, with a Deep Set and with a plain network on the list.

```python
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(0)
n_set, n_train = 10, 500
def make(m):                                   # sets of 10 numbers; target = their variance
    X = torch.randn(m, n_set) * torch.rand(m, 1) * 2
    return X, X.var(dim=1, unbiased=False)
Xtr, ytr = make(n_train)
Xte, yte = make(2000)

class DeepSet(torch.nn.Module):                # rho( sum_i phi(x_i) )
    def __init__(self, h=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.phi = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(1, h), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(h, h))
        self.rho = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(h, h), torch.nn.ReLU(),
                                       torch.nn.Linear(h, 1))
    def forward(self, X):
        return self.rho(self.phi(X.unsqueeze(-1)).sum(dim=1)).squeeze(-1)

mlp = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(n_set, 128), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(128, 128),
                          torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(128, 1), torch.nn.Flatten(0))
for name, net in [("Deep Set", DeepSet()), ("MLP on the list", mlp)]:
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
    for step in range(1500):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = torch.mean((net(Xtr) - ytr) ** 2)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        mse = torch.mean((net(Xte) - yte) ** 2).item()
        perm = torch.randperm(n_set)
        gap = (net(Xte) - net(Xte[:, perm])).abs().max().item()
    print(f"{name:16s} params {sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters()):6d}  "
          f"test MSE {mse:.4f}  max |f(x) - f(permuted x)| {gap:.1e}")
print("variance of the targets:", yte.var().item())
```

With 500 training sets, the Deep Set (8 513 parameters) reaches a test error twenty times smaller than the plain network (18 049 parameters), whose output changes when the list is reordered:
$$
\text{Deep Set: MSE } 0.0032,\ \text{gap } 10^{-6}; \qquad \text{plain network: MSE } 0.0700,\ \text{gap } 1.4 .
$$
The targets have variance 1.94. The plain network must learn the invariance from examples; the Deep Set has it for free.

### 2.4 Networks on graphs: graph attention

A message-passing network (Gilmer and coauthors, 2017) updates each node from an invariant aggregation of its neighbours: a Deep Set over every neighbourhood. Graph attention chooses the aggregation weights from the features.

::: def
[Definition 2.8 — Graph attention layer (Veličković and coauthors, 2018)]{.tag}
Let node $i$ carry features $h_i \in \mathbb{R}^F$ and let $\mathcal{N}(i)$ be its neighbours, $i$ included.

Take a weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{F' \times F}$ and a vector $a \in \mathbb{R}^{2F'}$, and write $\Vert$ for concatenation:
$$
e_{ij} = \operatorname{LeakyReLU}\big(a^\top [W h_i \,\Vert\, W h_j]\big), \qquad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp e_{ij}}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \exp e_{ik}}, \qquad h_i' = \sigma\Big(\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \alpha_{ij} W h_j\Big).
$$
Several heads are computed independently and concatenated, or averaged in the last layer.
:::

The layer is equivariant to relabelling the nodes, by the argument of Proposition 2.4 restricted to neighbourhoods. Its cost is linear in the number of edges, and it applies to graphs unseen in training.

The graph convolutional network of Kipf and Welling (2017) uses fixed weights given by the degrees; graph attention learns them. Brody, Alon and Yahav (2022) showed that this attention is *static*: the ranking of the neighbours by $e_{ij}$ is the same for every node $i$. They proposed a dynamic variant, GATv2.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::

-   Residual blocks keep the singular values of the input–output Jacobian near 1 (Proposition 2.1); normalised layers are scale-invariant (Proposition 2.2).
-   Self-attention is permutation-equivariant (Proposition 2.4): order comes only from positional encodings.
-   Every set function on a countable domain has the form $\rho(\sum \phi)$ (Theorem 2.6); linear equivariant layers are $aI + b\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ (Proposition 2.7).
-   Graph attention learns neighbour weights from features (Definition 2.8); building the symmetry in saves data (Code 2.1).
::::

## 3. Interpretability, visualisation and biases {#ch3}

A network that predicts well may be right for the wrong reasons: a hiring model that reads gender, a captioning model that says “man” because it sees a snowboard. This chapter gives tools to look inside a trained model, axioms to judge these tools, and methods to detect and reduce an undesired dependence on a sensitive attribute.

### 3.1 Attributions and their axioms

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Attribution]{.tag}
A **local explanation** of a model $f$ at an input $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, relative to a baseline $x'$, is a vector $A(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

Its component $i$ measures the contribution of feature $i$ to $f(x) - f(x')$. Sundararajan, Taly and Yan (2017) ask for three properties.

-   **Completeness**: the components sum to $f(x) - f(x')$.
-   **Sensitivity**: if $x$ and $x'$ differ in feature $i$ only and $f(x) \ne f(x')$, then $A_i(x) \ne 0$.
-   **Implementation invariance**: two networks that compute the same function receive the same attributions.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.2 — Gradient maps]{.tag}
The **saliency map** of Simonyan, Vedaldi and Zisserman (2014) is $|\partial f / \partial x_i|$, and **gradient × input** is $x_i\, \partial f / \partial x_i$.
:::

For a linear model and the baseline 0, gradient × input is complete. For a network it is not, because of saturation. The function $f(x) = \min(1, x)$ has zero derivative at $x = 2$, although $f(2) - f(0) = 1$: the gradient misses a feature that matters.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Integrated gradients are complete]{.tag}
Define the **integrated gradients** along the segment from $x'$ to $x$ by
$$
\mathrm{IG}_i(x) = (x_i - x'_i) \int_0^1 \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\big(x' + \alpha (x - x')\big)\, d\alpha .
$$
If $f$ is continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable along the segment, which holds for ReLU networks,
$$
\sum_{i=1}^d \mathrm{IG}_i(x) = f(x) - f(x').
$$

::: proof
Let $\gamma(\alpha) = x' + \alpha(x - x')$. The function $\alpha \mapsto f(\gamma(\alpha))$ is absolutely continuous, with derivative $\nabla f(\gamma(\alpha))^\top (x - x')$ almost everywhere. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives
$$
f(x) - f(x') = \int_0^1 \nabla f(\gamma(\alpha))^\top (x - x')\, d\alpha = \sum_i \mathrm{IG}_i(x).
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Sensitivity follows: if only feature $i$ differs, $\mathrm{IG}_i = f(x) - f(x')$. In practice the integral is a Riemann sum over 50 to 300 points, and completeness is the numerical check that the sum is fine enough.

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — Visualising convolutional networks]{.tag}

-   **Grad-CAM** (Selvaraju and coauthors, 2017). With feature maps $A^k$ of the last convolutional layer and class score $y^c$, weight each map by its average gradient $\alpha_k$; the map is $\operatorname{ReLU}(\sum_k \alpha_k A^k)$, upsampled to the image.
-   **Occlusion** (Zeiler and Fergus, 2014). Slide a grey patch over the image and record the drop of the class score.
-   **Activation maximisation** (Erhan, Bengio, Courville and Vincent, 2009). Find by gradient ascent an input that maximises a unit, with a regulariser that keeps it natural.
:::

Explanations must be tested like any estimator. Adebayo and coauthors (2018) randomise the weights of a trained network, layer by layer: a method whose map barely changes explains the input, its edges for instance, not the model. Guided backpropagation fails this sanity check; plain gradients and Grad-CAM pass it. Shapley values (Lundberg and Lee, 2017) are treated in [Multimodal Explainable AI](../s2-multimodal-xai/index.html).

### 3.2 Biases: definitions and proxies

Let $A$ be a sensitive attribute, such as gender, $Y$ the true outcome and $\hat Y$ the decision of the model.

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Fairness criteria]{.tag}

-   **Demographic parity**: $\hat Y$ is independent of $A$. The *parity gap* is
    $$
    \mathbb{P}(\hat Y = 1 \mid A = 1) - \mathbb{P}(\hat Y = 1 \mid A = 0).
    $$
-   **Equalised odds** (Hardt, Price and Srebro, 2016): $\hat Y$ is independent of $A$ given $Y$.
-   **Counterfactual test**: changing $A$ in the input, all else fixed, does not change $\hat Y$.
:::

When the base rates of the groups differ, these criteria cannot all hold for a non-trivial predictor (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, 2017; Chouldechova, 2017). The choice belongs to the application, not to the algorithm.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Unawareness is not fairness]{.tag}
Removing $A$ from the inputs does not give demographic parity. Let $A \in \{0, 1\}$ be balanced, $X = A + N$ with $N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, s^2)$ independent of $A$, and $\hat Y = \mathbb{1}[X > 1/2]$. Then the parity gap is
$$
2\,\Phi\Big(\frac{1}{2s}\Big) - 1 > 0 .
$$

::: proof
The two acceptance rates are
$$
\mathbb{P}(\hat Y = 1 \mid A = 1) = \mathbb{P}(N > -1/2) = \Phi\Big(\frac{1}{2s}\Big), \qquad \mathbb{P}(\hat Y = 1 \mid A = 0) = \mathbb{P}(N > 1/2) = 1 - \Phi\Big(\frac{1}{2s}\Big).
$$
Subtract. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $s = 0.5$ the gap is $2\Phi(1) - 1 = 0.683$, although $\hat Y$ never reads $A$: the feature $X$ is a **proxy**. A postcode, a sport or a first name plays this role in a CV.

Code 3.1 audits a CV-screening network trained on synthetic past decisions that favoured one gender, with a proxy feature correlated with gender. It measures the parity gap, the counterfactual test and integrated gradients.

```python
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(0)
m = 4000
g = torch.randint(0, 2, (m,)).float()                    # sensitive attribute (0 or 1)
skill, exper = torch.randn(m), torch.randn(m)
proxy = g + 0.5 * torch.randn(m)                         # e.g. a club membership correlated with g
y = (skill + 0.5 * exper + 0.8 * g + 0.5 * torch.randn(m) > 0.5).float()   # biased past decisions
names = ["skill", "experience", "proxy", "gender"]

def train(X):
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(X.shape[1], 32), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(32, 1))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    for _ in range(300):
        opt.zero_grad()
        torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(net(X).squeeze(1), y).backward()
        opt.step()
    return net

def integrated_gradients(net, x, base, steps=256):       # Riemann sum along the segment base -> x
    t = (torch.arange(steps) + 0.5).unsqueeze(1) / steps
    path = (base + t * (x - base)).requires_grad_(True)
    torch.sigmoid(net(path)).sum().backward()
    return (x - base) * path.grad.mean(0)

for k, cols in [(4, "with gender"), (3, "gender removed")]:
    X = torch.stack([skill, exper, proxy, g], 1)[:, :k]
    net = train(X)
    with torch.no_grad():
        yhat = (net(X).squeeze(1) > 0).float()
        dp = yhat[g == 1].mean() - yhat[g == 0].mean()
        Xf = X.clone()
        if k == 4:
            Xf[:, 3] = 1 - Xf[:, 3]                       # counterfactual: flip the attribute only
        flips = ((net(Xf).squeeze(1) > 0).float() != yhat).float().mean()
    base = X.mean(0)
    ig = torch.stack([integrated_gradients(net, X[i], base) for i in range(200)])
    gap = (torch.sigmoid(net(X[:200])).squeeze(1) - torch.sigmoid(net(base))).detach() - ig.sum(1)
    print(f"{cols:15s} parity gap {dp:.3f}  counterfactual flips {flips:.3f}  "
          f"mean |IG| " + " ".join(f"{n} {v:.3f}" for n, v in zip(names, ig.abs().mean(0))) +
          f"  completeness error {gap.abs().max():.1e}")
```

With gender as an input, the model reproduces the historical bias: a parity gap of 0.258, and 26 % of the decisions change when only gender is flipped. Gender receives a mean attribution of 0.242.

Without gender, the counterfactual test passes trivially, yet the parity gap is still 0.144. The attribution of the proxy rises tenfold:
$$
\text{mean } |\mathrm{IG}_{\text{proxy}}| :\ 0.016 \ \longrightarrow\ 0.161 .
$$
The bias has moved to the proxy, and the attributions show where. Completeness holds to $10^{-3}$.

### 3.3 Reducing biases

Hendricks, Burns, Saenko, Darrell and Rohrbach (2018) observed that image-captioning models trained on COCO guess gender from context, a snowboard for a man or a kitchen for a woman. They even amplify the imbalance of the training set, as Zhao and coauthors (2017) measured for visual recognition.

Their **Equalizer** adds two losses to the captioning loss.

-   An *appearance confusion* loss, on images where the person is masked out, asks for equal probabilities of the words “man” and “woman”: without the person, the model should not know.
-   A *confident* loss, on the full images, asks for a confident gender word when the person is visible.

They evaluate the error on gender words, the ratio of predicted to true gender proportions, and a pointing game: does the Grad-CAM map of the word “woman” fall on the person? The Equalizer reduces the error and moves the maps onto the people: right for the right reasons.

Other levers act on the data, by reweighting the training set so that $A$ and $Y$ become independent, or on the decision, with group-wise thresholds that equalise the odds (Hardt and coauthors, 2016). Or they act on training, adversarially.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.7 — Adversarial debiasing reaches demographic parity]{.tag}
An adversary predicts $A$ from $\hat Y$ with a conditional distribution $q(a \mid \hat y)$ and the cross-entropy loss. Its smallest possible loss is the conditional entropy $H(A \mid \hat Y)$, and
$$
H(A \mid \hat Y) = H(A) \iff \hat Y \text{ is independent of } A .
$$

::: proof
For any $q$, the expected loss is $H(A \mid \hat Y)$ plus the expected Kullback–Leibler divergence between the true conditional of $A$ given $\hat Y$ and $q$; it is minimal at the true conditional. Then $H(A \mid \hat Y) = H(A) - I(A; \hat Y)$, and the mutual information vanishes exactly under independence. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Zhang, Lemoine and Mitchell (2018) train the predictor to minimise its loss while maximising the loss of such an adversary. Giving the adversary $Y$ as an extra input targets equalised odds instead.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::

-   Gradients saturate; integrated gradients are complete (Theorem 3.3), and every attribution method should pass randomisation sanity checks.
-   Grad-CAM, occlusion and activation maximisation visualise what a convolutional network uses.
-   Fairness criteria conflict; removing the sensitive attribute leaves its proxies (Proposition 3.6).
-   Counterfactual tests and attributions audit a model (Code 3.1); the Equalizer and adversarial debiasing (Proposition 3.7) reduce the dependence.
::::

## 4. Small or noisy data: forms of weak supervision {#ch4}

Benchmarks offer many clean labels; real projects rarely do. Labels are few, coarse or wrong, and at the other extreme data are so plentiful that the question becomes how to spend the compute. This chapter treats each case.

### 4.1 Three forms of weak supervision

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Forms of weak supervision (Zhou, 2018)]{.tag}

-   **Incomplete**: only a subset of the data is labelled (semi-supervised and active learning).
-   **Inexact**: labels are coarser than the prediction, for instance one label per bag of instances or per image for a segmentation task.
-   **Inaccurate**: some labels are wrong.
:::

### 4.2 Few labels

The first tool is transfer: fine-tune a network pre-trained on a large data set, possibly without labels, as in the semester-1 [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) course. Data augmentation encodes known invariances (ch. 5). Then the unlabelled data can help, under the *cluster assumption*: the decision boundary should cross regions of low density.

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Pseudo-labelling with consistency (FixMatch)]{.tag}
Let $\alpha$ be a weak augmentation, $\mathcal{A}$ a strong one, $\tau$ a threshold (0.95 in the paper) and $p(\cdot)$ the predicted class probabilities. On an unlabelled input $u$, with the pseudo-label $\hat q = \arg\max_k p_k(\alpha(u))$, FixMatch (Sohn and coauthors, 2020) adds to the supervised loss the term
$$
\lambda_u\, \mathbb{1}\Big[\max_k p_k(\alpha(u)) \ge \tau\Big]\ \mathrm{CE}\big(\hat q,\ p(\mathcal{A}(u))\big).
$$
:::

Confident predictions on easy views become targets for hard views. Entropy minimisation (Grandvalet and Bengio, 2005) is the soft version: it pushes the predictions on unlabelled data towards confidence, hence the boundary away from the data. Active learning chooses instead which points to label, for instance the most uncertain ones (Settles, 2009).

### 4.3 Noisy labels

A network eventually memorises wrong labels, as the random labels of ch. 1 show. Arpit and coauthors (2017) observed that it fits the clean, simple patterns first, so early stopping helps. Two loss-level remedies have guarantees.

Assume class-conditional noise: the observed label $\tilde y$ equals $j$ with probability $T_{ij}$ when the clean label is $i$, independently of $x$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — Forward loss correction is consistent (Patrini and coauthors, 2017)]{.tag}
Let $T$ be invertible and let the model output a clean posterior $p(x)$. Train it with the cross-entropy of the corrected prediction $T^\top p(x)$ against the noisy labels. Over all functions $p$, the population loss is minimised by the clean posterior
$$
p(x) = \big(\mathbb{P}(y = k \mid x)\big)_{k = 1, \dots, K}.
$$

::: proof
1.  Let $\eta(x)$ be the clean posterior. The noisy posterior is $T^\top \eta(x)$, since $\mathbb{P}(\tilde y = j \mid x) = \sum_i T_{ij}\, \eta_i(x)$.
2.  At each $x$, the expected cross-entropy $\mathbb{E}[-\log q_{\tilde y}]$ over distributions $q$ is minimal exactly at the noisy posterior (Gibbs' inequality).
3.  The choice $q = T^\top p(x)$ reaches it with $p = \eta$, and only then, since $T^\top$ is injective. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In practice $T$ is estimated, for instance from *anchor points*: inputs that surely belong to class $i$, where the noisy posterior gives the row $i$ of $T$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Symmetric losses are noise-tolerant (Ghosh, Kumar and Sastry, 2017)]{.tag}
Assume uniform noise: with probability $\eta$, the label is replaced by one of the $K - 1$ other classes, chosen uniformly. Let the loss be **symmetric**: $\sum_{k=1}^K \ell(f(x), k) = C$ for every $f$ and $x$. Then the noisy risk is
$$
R_\eta(f) = \Big(1 - \frac{\eta K}{K - 1}\Big) R(f) + \frac{\eta\, C}{K - 1},
$$
so for $\eta < (K - 1)/K$ the noisy and clean risks have the same minimisers.

::: proof
Conditioning on the clean label $y$,
$$
R_\eta(f) = \mathbb{E}\Big[(1 - \eta)\, \ell(f(x), y) + \frac{\eta}{K - 1} \sum_{k \ne y} \ell(f(x), k)\Big].
$$
By symmetry the inner sum is $C - \ell(f(x), y)$. Collect the terms: the coefficient of $R(f)$ is $1 - \eta - \eta/(K-1)$, positive exactly when $\eta < (K-1)/K$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The mean absolute error between $p$ and the one-hot label, $2(1 - p_y)$, is symmetric with $C = 2(K - 1)$; the cross-entropy is not. The price is slow training, which the generalised cross-entropy of Zhang and Sabuncu (2018) trades against robustness.

Code 4.1 resamples 60 % of the training labels of the digits uniformly, so that 55 % end up wrong, and compares three losses on the clean test set.

```python
import torch
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
torch.set_num_threads(1)
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X = torch.tensor(X / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, torch.tensor(y), test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
K, eta = 10, 0.6                                          # 60 % of the labels resampled
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
flip = torch.rand(len(ytr), generator=g) < eta
y_noisy = torch.where(flip, torch.randint(0, K, (len(ytr),), generator=g), ytr)
T = (1 - eta) * torch.eye(K) + eta / K                    # T[i, j] = P(noisy = j | clean = i)
print(f"labels actually wrong: {(y_noisy != ytr).float().mean():.3f}")

def loss_ce(logits, t):
    return torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits, t)
def loss_forward(logits, t):                              # cross-entropy of T^T p against noisy labels
    p_noisy = torch.softmax(logits, 1) @ T
    return torch.nn.functional.nll_loss(torch.log(p_noisy), t)
def loss_mae(logits, t):                                  # || p - e_t ||_1 = 2 (1 - p_t): symmetric
    return (2 - 2 * torch.softmax(logits, 1).gather(1, t[:, None])).mean()

for name, loss_fn in [("cross-entropy", loss_ce), ("forward-corrected", loss_forward), ("MAE", loss_mae)]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(64, 256), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(256, K))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
    accs = []
    for step in range(1, 801):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss_fn(net(Xtr), y_noisy).backward()
        opt.step()
        if step in (100, 800):
            with torch.no_grad():
                accs.append((net(Xte).argmax(1) == yte).float().mean().item())
    with torch.no_grad():
        fit = (net(Xtr).argmax(1) == y_noisy).float().mean().item()
    print(f"{name:18s} clean test acc after 100 steps {accs[0]:.3f}, after 800 steps {accs[1]:.3f};"
          f"  agreement with noisy train labels {fit:.3f}")
```

The cross-entropy memorises every noisy label, and its test accuracy collapses from 0.744 at step 100 to 0.463. The two corrected losses do not memorise:
$$
\text{forward correction: } 0.813 \to 0.722, \qquad \text{MAE: } 0.844 \to 0.811 .
$$

### 4.4 Inexact labels: multiple-instance learning

In multiple-instance learning (Dietterich, Lathrop and Lozano-Pérez, 1997), a bag of instances is positive if at least one instance is. A histology slide labelled “tumour”, cut into thousands of unlabelled tiles, is a typical case. A bag classifier must be permutation-invariant, so by Theorem 2.6 it pools instance embeddings $h_i$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Attention pooling interpolates between mean and max]{.tag}
Let the instances have scores $s_i$ and embeddings $h_i$, and pool them with weights $a_i = \operatorname{softmax}(\beta s)_i$ into $z_\beta = \sum_i a_i h_i$.

Then $z_0$ is the mean of the $h_i$, and, if the maximal score is attained at a single instance $i^\star$,
$$
z_\beta \longrightarrow h_{i^\star} \qquad (\beta \to \infty).
$$

::: proof
At $\beta = 0$ all weights equal $1/m$. For $i \ne i^\star$, $a_i / a_{i^\star} = e^{\beta (s_i - s_{i^\star})} \to 0$, so $a_{i^\star} \to 1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Ilse, Tomczak and Welling (2018) learn the scores with a small network. The weights then localise the positive instances, which gives an explanation of the bag label for free.

### 4.5 Big data: scaling laws

With abundant data, the test loss of language models follows power laws in the number of parameters $N$ and of training tokens $D$ (Kaplan and coauthors, 2020). Hoffmann and coauthors (2022) fit, for a training compute $C \approx 6ND$ floating-point operations,
$$
L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}} .
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.6 — Compute-optimal allocation]{.tag}
Minimising $L(N, D)$ under the constraint $6ND = C$ gives
$$
N_{\mathrm{opt}} \propto C^{\beta / (\alpha + \beta)}, \qquad D_{\mathrm{opt}} \propto C^{\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)}.
$$

::: proof
Substitute $D = C/(6N)$ and set to zero the derivative in $N$ of $A N^{-\alpha} + B\, (6N/C)^{\beta}$. This gives
$$
\alpha A N^{-\alpha - 1} = \beta B\, 6^{\beta} N^{\beta - 1} C^{-\beta},
$$
so that $N^{\alpha + \beta}$ is proportional to $C^{\beta}$; then $D = C/(6N)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With similar exponents, parameters and data should grow together. Their 70-billion-parameter model Chinchilla, trained on 1.4 trillion tokens (20 tokens per parameter), outperformed larger models trained on fewer tokens. At that scale the bottleneck moves to data quality: deduplication, filtering and the label noise of web data. [Training and Deploying Large-Scale Models](../s2-training-deploying-large-models/index.html) covers the systems side.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::

-   Weak supervision is incomplete, inexact or inaccurate (Definition 4.1); each form has its tools.
-   Few labels: transfer, augmentation, then pseudo-labels with consistency (Definition 4.2).
-   Noisy labels: forward correction recovers the clean posterior (Theorem 4.3), symmetric losses tolerate uniform noise (Theorem 4.4), and plain cross-entropy memorises.
-   Bags of instances need invariant pooling; attention pooling sits between mean and max (Proposition 4.5).
-   With big data, compute-optimal training scales parameters and tokens together (Proposition 4.6).
::::

## 5. Modelling: deep learning, physics and control {#ch5}

In science much is known before any data is seen: symmetries, conservation laws, equations. This chapter injects that knowledge at three levels, the architecture, the loss and the structure of the model. It ends with reinforcement learning, where the network collects its own data.

### 5.1 Known invariances

Let a group $G$ act on the inputs. A model is **invariant** if $f(g \cdot x) = f(x)$ for all $g$, and **equivariant** if its output transforms along with the input. Data augmentation teaches an invariance approximately; an architecture can enforce it exactly.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.1 — Symmetrisation never hurts]{.tag}
Let $G$ be finite, the input distribution $G$-invariant and the regression function $f^\star$ invariant. The average $\bar f(x) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} f(g \cdot x)$ is invariant, and its excess squared risk is no larger than that of $f$:
$$
\mathbb{E}\big(\bar f(x) - f^\star(x)\big)^2 \le \mathbb{E}\big(f(x) - f^\star(x)\big)^2 .
$$

::: proof
Invariance: replacing $x$ by $h \cdot x$ permutes the terms of the sum. For the risk, $f^\star(x) = f^\star(g \cdot x)$, so by Jensen's inequality
$$
\big(\bar f(x) - f^\star(x)\big)^2 \le \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_g \big(f(g\cdot x) - f^\star(g \cdot x)\big)^2 .
$$
Take expectations: since $g \cdot x$ has the law of $x$, each term has the expectation of the right-hand side of the claim. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Group convolutions are equivariant (Cohen and Welling, 2016)]{.tag}
Let $G$ act on the pixel grid, for instance by translations and rotations of $90°$. For an image $f$ and a filter $\psi$, define the lifting correlation $[f \star \psi](g) = \sum_y f(y)\, \psi(g^{-1} y)$, and the action $(L_h f)(y) = f(h^{-1} y)$. Then
$$
(L_h f) \star \psi = L_h\, (f \star \psi).
$$

::: proof
Substitute $y = h y'$:
$$
[(L_h f) \star \psi](g) = \sum_{y'} f(y')\, \psi(g^{-1} h y') = [f \star \psi](h^{-1} g),
$$
which is $L_h(f \star \psi)$ evaluated at $g$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The ordinary convolution is the case of translations. Rotating the input of a group-convolutional network rotates its feature maps, instead of producing unrelated ones.

### 5.2 Physics as a loss: solving PDEs with networks

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Deep Galerkin Method (Sirignano and Spiliopoulos, 2018)]{.tag}
To solve $\partial_t u + \mathcal{N}[u] = 0$ on $[0, T] \times \Omega$, with $u = g$ on the boundary and $u(0, \cdot) = u_0$, represent $u$ by a network $u_\theta(t, x)$ and minimise
$$
J(\theta) = \big\|\partial_t u_\theta + \mathcal{N}[u_\theta]\big\|^2_{[0,T] \times \Omega} + \|u_\theta - g\|^2_{[0,T] \times \partial\Omega} + \|u_\theta(0, \cdot) - u_0\|^2_{\Omega} .
$$
Each squared norm is estimated at points drawn at random at every step, and derivatives come from automatic differentiation.
:::

No mesh is needed, which makes the method usable in high dimension. Physics-informed neural networks (Raissi, Perdikaris and Karniadakis, 2019) use the same residual loss and add observed data, which also solves inverse problems. [Learning Physical Phenomena](../s2-physics-learning-uq/index.html) develops them.

Why should a small residual mean a small error? This needs a stability estimate for the PDE.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — For the Poisson equation, the residual controls the error]{.tag}
Let $u^\star$ solve $-u'' = f$ on $(0, 1)$ with $u(0) = u(1) = 0$.

Let $v$ be smooth with the same boundary values, and let $r = -v'' - f$ be its residual. In $L^2$ norms, the error $e = v - u^\star$ satisfies
$$
\|e'\| \le \frac{1}{\pi}\, \|r\|, \qquad \|e\| \le \frac{1}{\pi^2}\, \|r\| .
$$

::: proof
The error solves $-e'' = r$ with $e(0) = e(1) = 0$. Multiply by $e$ and integrate by parts; the boundary terms vanish:
$$
\|e'\|^2 = \int_0^1 r\, e \le \|r\|\, \|e\| \le \frac{1}{\pi}\, \|r\|\, \|e'\|,
$$
by the Poincaré inequality $\|e\| \le \|e'\| / \pi$ on $(0, 1)$. Divide by $\|e'\|$, then apply Poincaré once more. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Code 5.1 solves this equation for $f(x) = \pi^2 \sin(\pi x)$, whose solution is $\sin(\pi x)$, with random collocation points at every step.

```python
import math
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(0)
# Solve -u'' = pi^2 sin(pi x) on (0, 1), u(0) = u(1) = 0; exact solution u(x) = sin(pi x).
net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(1, 32), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(32, 32),
                          torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(32, 1))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(opt, step_size=1000, gamma=0.2)
xb = torch.tensor([[0.0], [1.0]])                          # boundary points

def residual(x):                                           # r = -u'' - f, by automatic differentiation
    x = x.requires_grad_(True)
    u = net(x)
    du = torch.autograd.grad(u.sum(), x, create_graph=True)[0]
    d2u = torch.autograd.grad(du.sum(), x, create_graph=True)[0]
    return -d2u - math.pi ** 2 * torch.sin(math.pi * x)

for step in range(1, 3001):
    x = torch.rand(128, 1)                                 # fresh random collocation points (DGM)
    loss = residual(x).pow(2).mean() + 10 * net(xb).pow(2).mean()
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    sched.step()
    if step % 1000 == 0:
        xs = torch.linspace(0, 1, 1001).unsqueeze(1)
        err = (net(xs) - torch.sin(math.pi * xs)).abs().max().item()
        print(f"step {step}  loss {loss.item():.2e}  max |u_net - u| on a grid {err:.2e}")
```

After 3 000 steps the maximal error on a grid of 1 001 points is
$$
\max_x |u_\theta(x) - \sin(\pi x)| = 3.8 \times 10^{-4}.
$$
With a source of high frequency the same network fails; Exercise 18 explores this spectral bias.

### 5.3 Physical structure: Hamiltonian networks

A conservative mechanical system has an energy $H(q, p)$ and obeys Hamilton's equations. Greydanus, Dzamba and Yosinski (2019) learn a scalar network $H_\theta$ and define the dynamics from it, instead of predicting the velocities directly.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — A Hamiltonian network conserves its learnt energy]{.tag}
Let the model dynamics be $\dot q = \partial_p H_\theta$ and $\dot p = -\partial_q H_\theta$. Along every trajectory,
$$
\frac{d}{dt} H_\theta(q, p) = 0 .
$$

::: proof
By the chain rule and the two equations of the model,
$$
\frac{d}{dt} H_\theta = \partial_q H_\theta\, \dot q + \partial_p H_\theta\, \dot p = \partial_q H_\theta\, \partial_p H_\theta - \partial_p H_\theta\, \partial_q H_\theta = 0 .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A network that predicts $(\dot q, \dot p)$ without this structure drifts in energy over long rollouts. The numerical integrator matters too: Exercise 16 compares explicit and symplectic Euler.

### 5.4 Reinforcement learning: the network collects its own data

In a Markov decision process with rewards $r(s, a)$ and discount $\gamma < 1$, the optimal action-value function is the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator
$$
(\mathcal{T} Q)(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{s' \mid s, a}\, \max_{a'} Q(s', a').
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.6 — The Bellman operator is a contraction]{.tag}
For bounded $Q_1, Q_2$, in the supremum norm,
$$
\|\mathcal{T} Q_1 - \mathcal{T} Q_2\|_\infty \le \gamma\, \|Q_1 - Q_2\|_\infty .
$$

::: proof
For every next state $s'$,
$$
\big|\max_{a'} Q_1(s', a') - \max_{a'} Q_2(s', a')\big| \le \max_{a'} |Q_1(s', a') - Q_2(s', a')| .
$$
Take the expectation and multiply by $\gamma$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 5.7 — Deep Q-network (Mnih and coauthors, 2015)]{.tag}
A network $Q_\theta$ minimises, over transitions $(s, a, r, s')$ drawn from a **replay buffer** of past experience,
$$
\big(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q_{\theta^-}(s', a') - Q_\theta(s, a)\big)^2,
$$
where the **target network** $\theta^-$ is a copy of $\theta$ refreshed every few thousand steps.
:::

With these two devices the same network learnt 49 Atari games from pixels, at a level comparable to a professional games tester on many of them. They answer two practical difficulties. The data are not independent, because they depend on the current policy: the buffer decorrelates and reuses them. The targets move with $\theta$: freezing $\theta^-$ turns each phase into a regression.

Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data together, the *deadly triad* of Sutton and Barto (2018), can still diverge. The maximum over noisy estimates is biased upwards, which Double DQN corrects (van Hasselt, Guez and Silver, 2016). [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) treats the theory.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::

-   Averaging over a symmetry group never increases the excess risk when the target is invariant (Proposition 5.1); group convolutions build the symmetry in (Proposition 5.2).
-   A PDE becomes a loss on random collocation points (Definition 5.3); a stability estimate turns a small residual into a small error (Proposition 5.4).
-   Learning the Hamiltonian instead of the velocities conserves energy by construction (Proposition 5.5).
-   Deep Q-learning is regression on a contraction's fixed point, made stable by a replay buffer and a target network (Definition 5.7).
::::

## 6. Generative models: VAE, GAN and normalizing flows {#ch6}

A generative model learns a distribution $p_\theta$ close to that of the data, to sample from it or to evaluate densities. The three classical deep families differ in how they treat the likelihood: the variational auto-encoder bounds it, the adversarial network avoids it, the flow computes it exactly. Diffusion models appear in ch. 9 and in [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html).

### 6.1 Variational auto-encoders

A latent variable $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ is decoded by a network into $p_\theta(x \mid z)$. The likelihood $p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz$ is intractable, so an encoder $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ approximates the posterior (Kingma and Welling, 2014; Rezende, Mohamed and Wierstra, 2014).

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.1 — Evidence lower bound]{.tag}
For every encoder $q_\phi$,
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)} \log p_\theta(x \mid z) - \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\Vert\, p(z)\big)}_{\mathrm{ELBO}(\theta, \phi;\, x)} + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\Vert\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big).
$$
Hence the ELBO is a lower bound of the log-likelihood, tight when the encoder equals the true posterior.

::: proof
By Bayes' rule, for every $z$,
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \log p_\theta(x, z) - \log p_\theta(z \mid x).
$$
Add and subtract $\log q_\phi(z \mid x)$, then take the expectation over $q_\phi$. The two resulting terms are the ELBO and the last KL divergence, which is non-negative. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a Gaussian encoder with means $\mu_j$ and variances $\sigma_j^2$, the KL term has the closed form $\frac12 \sum_j (\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j^2)$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Reparameterisation]{.tag}
Write $z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. For a smooth function $h$ with integrable derivatives,
$$
\nabla_\phi\, \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\, h(z) = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}\, \nabla_\phi\, h\big(\mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon\big).
$$

::: proof
The law of $z$ is $q_\phi(\cdot \mid x)$, so the expectation equals
$$
\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon\, h(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \odot \varepsilon),
$$
where $\phi$ no longer appears in the distribution. Differentiate under the expectation, which dominated convergence allows. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

One sample of $\varepsilon$ per data point gives an unbiased, low-variance gradient of the ELBO. With a Gaussian decoder, samples tend to be blurry; with a powerful decoder, the encoder may be ignored, which is called *posterior collapse*.

### 6.2 Generative adversarial networks

A generator $G$ maps noise $z$ to samples, and a discriminator $D$ tells real from generated (Goodfellow and coauthors, 2014). They play
$$
\min_G \max_D\ V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\mathrm{d}}} \log D(x) + \mathbb{E}_{z} \log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big).
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Optimal discriminator and Jensen–Shannon divergence]{.tag}
Let $p_{\mathrm{g}}$ be the density of the generated samples. For a fixed generator, the best discriminator and the value of the game are
$$
D^\star = \frac{p_{\mathrm{d}}}{p_{\mathrm{d}} + p_{\mathrm{g}}}, \qquad V(D^\star, G) = -\log 4 + 2\, \mathrm{JS}(p_{\mathrm{d}} \Vert p_{\mathrm{g}}),
$$
which is minimal exactly when $p_{\mathrm{g}} = p_{\mathrm{d}}$.

::: proof
1.  The value is an integral over $x$,
    $$
    V = \int \big(p_{\mathrm{d}} \log D + p_{\mathrm{g}} \log(1 - D)\big)\, dx .
    $$
    For $a, b > 0$, the function $y \mapsto a \log y + b \log(1 - y)$ is maximal at $y = a/(a + b)$, which gives $D^\star$ pointwise.
2.  Substitute and introduce the mixture $m = (p_{\mathrm{d}} + p_{\mathrm{g}})/2$. The last two terms of
    $$
    V(D^\star, G) = -\log 4 + \mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{d}} \Vert m) + \mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{g}} \Vert m)
    $$
    are $2\,\mathrm{JS}$ by definition.
3.  The Jensen–Shannon divergence is non-negative and vanishes only for equal distributions. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In practice the generator maximises $\log D(G(z))$, which gives stronger gradients early in training. Training remains delicate: the generator may cover only a few modes (*mode collapse*). When the two distributions have disjoint supports, the Jensen–Shannon divergence is constant and its gradient carries no information. The Wasserstein GAN (Arjovsky, Chintala and Bottou, 2017) replaces it by a transport distance. GANs have no likelihood, so they are evaluated by sample statistics such as the Fréchet inception distance (Heusel and coauthors, 2017).

### 6.3 Normalizing flows

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — Change of variables]{.tag}
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ be a diffeomorphism and $z = f(x)$ have density $p_Z$. Then
$$
\log p_X(x) = \log p_Z\big(f(x)\big) + \log \big|\det J_f(x)\big| .
$$
For a composition of such maps, the log-determinants add.

::: proof
This is the change-of-variables formula for integrals, applied to $\mathbb{P}(X \in B) = \mathbb{P}(Z \in f(B))$ for every Borel set $B$; the second claim follows from the chain rule and the multiplicativity of determinants. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A flow trains by exact maximum likelihood and samples by inverting $f$. The difficulty is to build maps that are expressive, easy to invert, and have cheap determinants.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.5 — Affine coupling layers (Dinh, Sohl-Dickstein and Bengio, 2017)]{.tag}
Split $x = (x_a, x_b)$ and let $s, t$ be arbitrary networks. The map $y_a = x_a$, $y_b = x_b \odot e^{s(x_a)} + t(x_a)$ is invertible, with
$$
x_b = \big(y_b - t(y_a)\big) \odot e^{-s(y_a)}, \qquad \log |\det J| = \sum_j s_j(x_a).
$$

::: proof
Since $y_a = x_a$, the inverse is read off directly. The Jacobian is block lower-triangular, with the identity and $\operatorname{diag}(e^{s(x_a)})$ on the diagonal; its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The networks $s$ and $t$ are never inverted, so they can be as complex as needed. Code 6.1 stacks six coupling layers, alternating the coordinate left unchanged, and fits the two-moons data set of scikit-learn by maximum likelihood.

```python
import math
import torch
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(0)
X = torch.tensor(make_moons(3000, noise=0.05, random_state=0)[0], dtype=torch.float32)
X = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)
Xtr, Xte = X[:2000], X[2000:]

class Coupling(torch.nn.Module):            # y_a = x_a,  y_b = x_b * exp(s(x_a)) + t(x_a)
    def __init__(self, a):
        super().__init__()
        self.a, self.b = a, 1 - a
        self.net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(1, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(),
                                       torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 2))
    def forward(self, x):                   # data -> latent, with log |det Jacobian|
        s, t = self.net(x[:, [self.a]]).chunk(2, dim=1)
        s = torch.tanh(s)
        y = x.clone()
        y[:, [self.b]] = x[:, [self.b]] * torch.exp(s) + t
        return y, s.squeeze(1)
    def inverse(self, y):
        s, t = self.net(y[:, [self.a]]).chunk(2, dim=1)
        x = y.clone()
        x[:, [self.b]] = (y[:, [self.b]] - t) * torch.exp(-torch.tanh(s))
        return x

layers = torch.nn.ModuleList([Coupling(i % 2) for i in range(6)])
def log_prob(x):                            # change of variables: log p(x) = log N(f(x)) + log|det J_f(x)|
    logdet = torch.zeros(len(x))
    for layer in layers:
        x, ld = layer(x)
        logdet = logdet + ld
    return -0.5 * (x ** 2).sum(1) - math.log(2 * math.pi) + logdet

opt = torch.optim.Adam(layers.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
for step in range(1, 1201):
    batch = Xtr[torch.randint(0, len(Xtr), (256,))]
    loss = -log_prob(batch).mean()
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    if step % 400 == 0:
        with torch.no_grad():
            print(f"step {step}  test NLL per point {-log_prob(Xte).mean().item():.3f} nats")
with torch.no_grad():
    z = Xte.clone()
    for layer in layers:
        z, _ = layer(z)
    x_back = z
    for layer in reversed(layers):
        x_back = layer.inverse(x_back)
    print("max reconstruction error f^-1(f(x)) - x:", (x_back - Xte).abs().max().item())
    print("Gaussian fit of the same data, NLL:",
          (-torch.distributions.MultivariateNormal(Xtr.mean(0), torch.cov(Xtr.T)).log_prob(Xte).mean()).item())
```

On held-out points the flow reaches a negative log-likelihood of 1.27 nats per point, against 2.73 for the best Gaussian, and it inverts to $2 \times 10^{-6}$:
$$
\mathrm{NLL}_{\text{flow}} = 1.27 \ \text{nats} \quad < \quad \mathrm{NLL}_{\text{Gaussian}} = 2.73 \ \text{nats}.
$$

| | VAE | GAN | Normalizing flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| Likelihood | lower bound (ELBO) | none | exact |
| Latent space | smaller than the data | smaller than the data | same dimension as the data |
| Typical weakness | blurry samples, posterior collapse | mode collapse, unstable training | constrained architectures |

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 6
:::

-   The ELBO is the log-likelihood minus the KL gap of the encoder (Proposition 6.1); reparameterisation gives its gradient (Proposition 6.2).
-   Against the optimal discriminator, a GAN minimises a Jensen–Shannon divergence (Theorem 6.3), which explains both its equilibrium and its training troubles.
-   Flows compute exact likelihoods by the change of variables (Proposition 6.4); coupling layers make the determinant a sum (Proposition 6.5).
::::

## 7. Auto-ML: automatic hyper-parameter tuning {#ch7}

Learning rate, width, depth, weight decay, augmentation: a network has many hyper-parameters, and a published gain often owes as much to tuning as to the method. Auto-ML automates the search. This chapter gives the principles that make it efficient.

### 7.1 The problem

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Hyper-parameter optimisation is a bilevel problem]{.tag}
For hyper-parameters $\lambda$, training returns a minimiser $\theta^\star(\lambda)$ of $L_{\mathrm{train}}(\cdot, \lambda)$, and the goal is
$$
\lambda^\star \in \arg\min_\lambda\ L_{\mathrm{val}}\big(\theta^\star(\lambda), \lambda\big).
$$
:::

Each evaluation of the outer objective costs a full training run. The objective is noisy, often not differentiable, and has cheaper approximations: fewer epochs, a subset of the data, a smaller model.

### 7.2 Random versus grid search

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Why random search beats grid search (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012)]{.tag}

1.  With $n$ independent uniform trials, the probability that at least one falls in the best fraction $q$ of the search space is $1 - (1 - q)^n$.
2.  A grid of $n$ points in $d$ dimensions tries only $n^{1/d}$ values of each hyper-parameter; $n$ random points try $n$ distinct values of each, almost surely.

Hence, when the validation loss depends on few of the hyper-parameters, random search explores the ones that matter far better.

::: proof
1.  Each trial misses the best region with probability $1 - q$, independently of the others.
2.  A grid is a product of $d$ one-dimensional grids with $n^{1/d}$ values each. The coordinates of random points are continuous and independent, hence distinct with probability one. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $q = 5\%$, sixty trials suffice for a probability above 0.95:
$$
1 - 0.95^{60} = 0.954 .
$$

### 7.3 Bayesian optimisation

Bayesian optimisation fits a Gaussian-process surrogate to the evaluations made so far, with posterior mean $\mu(\lambda)$ and standard deviation $\sigma(\lambda)$, and evaluates next where an *acquisition function* is largest (Snoek, Larochelle and Adams, 2012).

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.3 — Expected improvement in closed form]{.tag}
Let $f^\star$ be the best value observed and $F(\lambda) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ the surrogate's belief at $\lambda$. With $z = (f^\star - \mu)/\sigma$, the expected improvement for minimisation is
$$
\mathrm{EI}(\lambda) = \mathbb{E}\big[\max(f^\star - F(\lambda), 0)\big] = (f^\star - \mu)\, \Phi(z) + \sigma\, \varphi(z).
$$

::: proof
Write $F = \mu + \sigma U$ with $U$ standard normal. The improvement is positive exactly when $U < z$, so
$$
\mathrm{EI} = \int_{-\infty}^{z} (f^\star - \mu - \sigma u)\, \varphi(u)\, du = (f^\star - \mu)\,\Phi(z) + \sigma\, \varphi(z),
$$
using $\int_{-\infty}^{z} u\, \varphi(u)\, du = -\varphi(z)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The first term rewards a low predicted loss (exploitation), the second a high uncertainty (exploration). Code 7.1 compares a $4 \times 4$ grid, random search and Bayesian optimisation with 16 evaluations each, on a validation-loss surface where only the first hyper-parameter matters, as is common for the learning rate.

```python
import warnings
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
```
